title: The honey teaching
hookLine: a secret teaching, once passed on by a sage with a horse's head: everything is honey for everything else
carry: one self in all, so all feed each other
tomorrow: Janaka's court: the thousand cows with gold horns
last: THE SALT ISN'T GONE; IT'S EVERYWHERE.

cards: Old Vedic stories tell of a sage named Dadhyanc who knew a secret teaching called the honey knowledge. The god Indra, the stories say, warned him: teach it to anyone, and I'll cut off your head.
Two divine twins, the Ashvins, wanted it badly. So they took off his head, gave him a horse's head, and he taught them through that. Indra struck it off, and the twins put his own head back.
The Brihadaranyaka quotes old hymns that remember the horse-headed teacher, and gives us the teaching itself, the one worth risking a head for.

teach.h: THE EARTH IS HONEY FOR ALL BEINGS.
teach.b: This earth, it says, is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth. Madhu: honey, sweetness, the thing that feeds. The earth feeds every creature, and every creature feeds the earth back.

teach.h: AGAIN AND AGAIN, THE SAME SHAPE.
teach.b: Then the same line, again and again, like a chant. Water is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for water. Fire.
Humankind. And last, the self. And each time the text adds: the shining, deathless person in that thing, and the shining, deathless person in you, are just this self.
That's the secret. Not a chain with a top and a bottom, but everything feeding everything, because the same self lives in both.
Then a picture: as the spokes of a wheel are all held in the hub and the rim, so all beings, all gods, all worlds are held in this self.

And near the end of the chapter, three short words that later teachers count among the great sayings of the Upanishads: ayam atma brahma. This self is Brahman. You can see the same idea in an old Hindu habit.

teach.h: A DAILY OFFERING TO ALL BEINGS.
teach.b: The dharma texts list five great daily offerings, and one of them is to all beings. Many homes still set out a little food for birds, a cow or a hungry animal before the family eats.

teach.h: ONE SELF IN ALL, SO ALL FEED EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Many teachers read it as the honey teaching made daily: you are fed by everything, so you feed something back.

how: The honey doctrine, madhu vidya, is studied as a meditation in the Vedanta tradition; ayam atma brahma, this self is Brahman, from its closing lines and from the Mandukya Upanishad, is counted among the great sayings, the mahavakyas.

o: a sweet offering placed before a deity
the nectar of deathlessness the gods drank
honey, sweetness: what every being is for others

games.q: what's inside the honey — tap the pairs.
p: taught it with a horse's head
all beings held in the self

s: the honey doctrine says only bees and flowers feed each other
earth, water, fire, wind, sun, truth, humankind, the self: each is honey for all, and all for it.
ayam atma brahma appears in this chapter
near its end (2.5.19); the same words are in the Mandukya Upanishad.
the text quotes old hymns about a horse-headed teacher
Dadhyanc, who taught the honey knowledge to the Ashvins.

games.q: you want a picture for how all beings, gods and worlds are held in one self. which does the text choose?
o: the spokes of a wheel in its hub and rim.
a river running to the sea.
games.why: spokes in the hub and rim. every spoke different, every one held in the same center.

practice: Name one thing that fed you today: food, water, sunlight, someone's patience, and let it be sweet.
Then turn it around and name one way you fed something back: the plant you watered, the friend you answered, the earth your breath went out to.
Go gently back and forth, fed by, feeding, and let the line in the text become a rhythm.

wordCard.voice: Madhu, honey, sweetness. The thing every being is for every other: the earth for us, and us for the earth.

orig.note: Sanskrit madhu: honey, sweetness, the thing that feeds.

carryVoice: Your line: one self in all, so all feed each other. Tomorrow, a thousand cows with gold on their horns. Until then.
